name: Urochloa
common_group: Signalgrasses — dense, spreading, and big-spikelet comparisons
look_here_first: START WITH THREE SIGNALGRASS HEADS: U. fusca has tight rather chunky spikelet clusters; U. reptans forms a much more delicate spreading narrow-branched head; U. texana has larger (~4.5–6 mm) spikelets along alternate ascending branches. These silhouettes HELP, but reliable separation depends on measuring mature spikelets and the proportion of the LOWER GLUME.

comparison_lesson.title: Urochloa practical installed-species field key
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: TIGHT/ROUND fusca; LOOSE/TINY reptans; LARGER SPIKELETS texana. Confirm lower glume proportion under 10–20×.
quick_split: Urochloa fusca — Native Texas signalgrass candidate with a TIGHT upright cluster of thick, short flowering branches carrying many blunt, plump 2.4–3 mm spikelets. Compare mature spikelet SIZE AND SHAPE, and small lower glume (~one-quarter to one-third of spikelet) with U. texana and U. reptans. The current image shows the tight head and broad blade, NOT glume structure.

Urochloa reptans — Introduced in many Texas floras. Look for an annual with decumbent or creeping rooted stems and a LOOSE spreading/ascending set of slender flowering racemes (unlike dense blunt-headed U. fusca). Measure a tiny ~1.5–2.5 mm ovoid spikelet and look for the almost missing basal glume; a seedhead photo alone does not show rooted basal nodes.

Urochloa texana — Native Texas signalgrass with comparatively BIG ovoid pointed spikelets (~4.5–6 mm), borne singly or in pairs along several ascending side branches of a terminal panicle. Check the lower glume (around half to two-thirds of spikelet length), cross-veined lower lemma and tough, transversely wrinkled upper fertile lemma. Whole-plant overview alone is not enough for confirmation.
guardrails: U. reptans is introduced in East Texas flora, whereas U. fusca and U. texana are treated as native at state scale; county reviews paused.
Former Brachiaria and Panicum combinations may refer to the same taxon—don't count synonyms twice.
The whole-plant Texas signalgrass image does not establish diagnostic spikelet anatomy.

key_characters: Warm-season signalgrass with several short, often erect or ascending, densely spikeleted flowering branches.
Plump blunt obovoid mature spikelets around 2.4–3 mm, one basal reduced/sterile floret and a fertile upper floret.
Lower glume generally small, about one-quarter to one-third total spikelet length.
Upper glume and sterile lower lemma with visible crossveins under magnification; upper fertile lemma tough and transversely wrinkled.
Soft broad grass blade, as seen in original source photo, but leaf width alone not diagnostic.
comparisons.against_group: U. reptans has looser, often spreading almost star-shaped branches and tiny short 2-mm spikelets, with a very small basal clasping glume. U. texana generally has larger ~4.5–6 mm pointed spikelets and more open, long alternating racemes, lower glume usually about two-thirds spikelet length. For native/introduced calls, show several ripe spikelets with scale rather than relying on the head silhouette.

key_characters: Usually creeping or ascending warm-season annual, frequently in disturbed moist sites.
Racemes relatively slender with spaced tiny spikelets rather than dense plump cylindrical clusters.
Spikelets much smaller (~1.5–2.5 mm) than U. texana; lower glume almost minute, ~15–25% of length.
Upper glume and sterile lemma occupy most of spikelet; tough fertile lemma and palea transversely wrinkled.
Creeping basal shoots may root at nodes; must be seen/photographed to assert.
comparisons.against_group: U. fusca tends to have densely clustered blunt plump spikelets ~2.4–3 mm. U. texana has comparatively large 4.5–6 mm elongated spikelets and looser ascending branches on a stouter habit. Compare with Digitaria ciliaris if fingerlike racemes dominate: paired spikelets and membranous ligule are relevant. The 'creeping' name alone does not identify a sterile individual.

key_characters: Warm-season native Texas grass; often an annual tuft of soft relatively broad foliage.
Terminal panicle generally with multiple alternate ascending principal branches, often 4 or more.
Spikelets distinctively large for this 3-way comparison, about 4.5–6 mm long; single or paired at branch nodes.
Lower glume often reaches near middle to ~two-thirds spikelet, unlike much smaller basal glumes of U. fusca or U. reptans.
Very short stalked spikelets, lower floret male/sterile and upper floret fertile; upper fertile lemma firm and finely cross-wrinkled.
True ligule and sheath anatomy need macro confirmation and should never be fabricated from habitat overview.
comparisons.against_group: U. fusca has plumper smaller ~2.4–3 mm spikelets in generally shorter densely packed flowering branches. U. reptans has tiny ~1.5–2.5 mm spikelets and loose slender branches plus decumbent growth. Other Paniceae may look similar; do not confirm solely from whole clump or 'signalgrass' common name. In this one existing wide photograph, detailed spikelets are too small to verify.

what_to_teach_crew: Every source picture used below is a real existing taxon-labelled project photo, not a generated illustration.
The panicle and leaf outline are entry cues. To assign native vs introduced correctly, photograph mature measured spikelets and exact collar of the SAME plant.
Never count source-labelled photos as expert re-determinations; a visible structure arrow is not proof of the complete taxon.
U. reptans is introduced in East Texas flora, whereas U. fusca and U. texana are treated as native at state scale; county reviews paused.
Former Brachiaria and Panicum combinations may refer to the same taxon—don't count synonyms twice.
The whole-plant Texas signalgrass image does not establish diagnostic spikelet anatomy.
